sentences.text: I built a RAG system that runs entirely on my laptop.
It ended up with a retrieval score of ninety-five percent.
But the interesting part isn't what worked.
Three of the techniques everyone recommends, HyDE, fine-tuning, and a better embedding model, did nothing.
And one tiny bug in a tool definition cut my results by sixty percent.
Here's the whole story, with the numbers.
The project is a help-desk assistant.
You describe an IT problem, and it searches past tickets and tells you what they say.
Everything is local on an M2 MacBook Pro.
Ollama runs the models: qwen3 eight-billion for generation and nomic for embeddings.
Qdrant is the vector database.
A cross-encoder reranks results.
Phoenix traces every step.
And at the end, ollmcp lets a local model decide when to search.
The data is a synthetic ticket dataset from Hugging Face, a thousand tickets in the free sample.
Here is the path a question takes.
It gets rewritten, then searched two ways at once, then grouped into distinct problems, reranked, filtered, and only then handed to the model.
First surprise.
A thousand tickets, but only fifty-six distinct problems.
Each one is repeated ten to thirty times with different names attached.
The comments are even worse: twenty-four distinct sentences, attached to tickets more or less at random.
And there is no real resolution field, so I can't trust any of it as a fix.
It's a ticket search and triage tool.
That one fact shaped almost every decision after this.
I searched for "printer" with three methods: embeddings, keyword search, and the two combined.
Every single result, in all three, was the same problem: label printer feeds blank stock.
But the data has three different printer problems.
The biggest cluster of near-duplicates filled the whole top of the list, and I'd never have known the other two existed.
Averages would have hidden this.
I only saw it by reading the actual results.
The fix was to stop retrieving tickets and start retrieving distinct problems.
Qdrant can group by a field, so I asked for the top twenty different summaries.
The chance that the right problem was even in the candidate pool jumped from seventy-four to ninety-five percent.
Then a cross-encoder reranker, reading the question and each summary together, took the right answer in the top five from about seventy to ninety-five percent.
One lesson inside that: reranking on the short summary beat reranking on the full ticket text, because the full text had random noise attached to it.
The real lesson: retrieval can't recover what it never fetched, so measure each stage separately.
Now the things that didn't work.
HyDE, where the model writes a fake answer to search with: no gain, and it got worse when I let it replace the question.
Fine-tuning the embedding model: it trained fine, and changed nothing, because the untouched model was already finding the right answer.
Switching to a better embedder: dramatically better on its own, and exactly the same once the reranker was in the pipeline.
The reranker erased the difference.
And a score cutoff I'd tuned by eye was silently throwing away correct results.
Components interact.
A win in isolation doesn't predict a win in the system.
How do you know any of this is real?
My first set of test questions was too easy: the model had paraphrased the ticket titles, and everything scored near perfect.
Useless.
Then I had a result that said ninety-five percent, and it was computed on only nineteen questions.
One question is worth five points.
To be confident one system really beats another, and isn't just lucky, you'd want something like six wins and no losses, not one win.
And if you see nineteen out of nineteen, the real failure rate could still be sixteen percent.
I wrote a guide on reading these numbers, and I'll link it.
One more thing I have to be upfront about: I tuned on the same questions I scored on, so these numbers are optimistic.
The scariest failure in RAG is the confident wrong answer.
So I added a floor on the reranker score.
Below it, the system doesn't even call the model.
It says there's no match and suggests opening a ticket, and that path takes under half a second.
In my tests it refused all seven questions it couldn't answer.
The cost: it also wrongly refused three of nineteen valid questions, about sixteen percent.
That's a trade-off you choose, not a bug you fix.
And I broke it once: I told the model to reply "no match" when unsure, and it refused eight of nineteen good questions.
Small models take instructions very literally.
Tracing shows where the time goes.
In a warm run it takes a few seconds, and the generator is roughly three quarters of that.
The query rewrite is about a fifth, and retrieval plus reranking barely register.
The first run after a cold start is slower, because the models have to load.
So if you want this faster, shrink the context or the model.
Don't optimize the retrieval.
Caveat: that's three traces, so treat the percentages as illustrative.
Last piece: ollmcp lets a local model decide when to search.
I exposed my pipeline as one tool.
In my tests it used the tool for all nineteen IT questions and none of the six chit-chat prompts.
But the first test found only six of nineteen correct tickets, versus sixteen in the pipeline.
The reason: the model was filling in an optional priority filter on every call, with a value nobody asked for, and that hid the right tickets.
I deleted the parameter and the results matched.
If you build tools for small models, keep the schema minimal.
Five things.
One: read your data before you pick techniques.
Two: measure every stage, because the pool limits everything after it.
Three: test components in the full system, not alone.
Four: report your sample size and be honest about tuning on your test set.
And five: decide up front which error costs more, wrong answers or refusals.
The code, commands, and the number-reading guide are linked below.
If you want a follow-up where I test this on questions I wrote blind, say so in the comments.
